The Great bustard (Otis tarda) is one of the heaviest flying birds on Earth, exhibiting extreme sexual dimorphism in adult body size. Females reach an asymptotic mass of 3816 grams [Wwi = 3816 grams], a value that reflects their comparatively streamlined body plan suited for seasonal migration and long-distance flights. Males, in stark contrast, attain a staggering ultimate wet weight of 11975 grams [Wwi = 11975 grams], making them nearly three times heavier than females and among the most mass-dimorphic of all avian species. This profound difference in body size is a cornerstone of the species' lekking mating system, where male mass is directly correlated with dominance and access to displaying grounds. The ecological implications of this dimorphism are substantial: females can exploit a broader range of foraging habitats due to their lighter frame, while males are more constrained by the need to support their enormous bulk, particularly during the energetically demanding breeding season.

Development in the Great bustard begins during a precisely timed incubation period. Field observations and captive breeding records indicate that eggs maintained at a consistent temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] hatch after approximately 24.5 days [ab = approximately 24.5 days], based on data reported by Tiel and Willemsen in 2002. This incubation duration is typical for a bird of this size and altricial developmental mode. Upon hatching, the precocial chicks emerge with a wet weight of 88.5 grams [Wwb = 88.5 grams], a mass that is already substantial and supports their rapid transition to independent foraging. The initial investment in egg production is considerable, with a freshly laid egg weighing around 143 grams [Ww0 = around 143 grams], representing a significant proportion of the female's own body mass and underscoring the energetic cost of reproduction at the very start of the life cycle.

The early life stages of the Great bustard are characterized by rapid growth and a series of critical developmental milestones. Under the typical thermal conditions of the active metabolic season for this species (40.25 °C [T = 40.25 °C]), fledging — the achievement of sustained flight — occurs at approximately 33.75 days after hatching [tx = approximately 33.75 days after hatching]. This is a remarkably short fledgling period for such a large bird, reflecting an accelerated growth strategy that minimizes the time chicks are vulnerable on the ground. Following this, the period leading to gonadal maturation is considerably longer. Puberty, defined as the onset of reproductive potential, is reached at 101.25 days after hatching [tp = 101.25 days after hatching] when evaluated at the same ambient temperature of 40.25 °C [T = 40.25 °C]. This interval allows for the completion of most somatic growth before the individual becomes reproductively competent, a life-history pattern typical of species that invest heavily in each offspring.

Reproductive maturity in Great bustards is not immediately followed by breeding; a significant delay exists before individuals attempt their first brood. The time elapsed since birth at first brood is 4.5 years [tR = 4.5 years] when measured under the thermal conditions of 40.25 °C [T = 40.25 °C]. This protracted pre-reproductive period is among the longest recorded for any bird of comparable size and is driven by the need for males, in particular, to attain the enormous body mass required to compete for mates on the lek. During these years, young birds hone their foraging skills and establish dominance hierarchies. The species' long-term survival strategy is further underscored by a maximum lifespan of 28.3 years [am = 28.3 years] at 40.25 °C [T = 40.25 °C], a longevity that permits multiple breeding opportunities across a lifetime and buffers against years of poor reproductive success.

Reproductive output in the Great bustard is modest, reflecting a slow life-history pace. Females typically lay 2.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.5 eggs per clutch], a small clutch size that is compensated for by the large size and high energy content of each egg. Furthermore, they produce only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a frequency that is low compared to many other grassland birds. This conservative reproductive strategy, with a maximum annual output of just 2.5 eggs [Ri = annual output of just 2.5 eggs], is a direct consequence of the considerable energetic demands of producing such large offspring and the extended period of post-hatching care. The population dynamics of the species are therefore highly sensitive to adult survival rates, as a single year of low fledging success cannot be quickly compensated for by a subsequent high-output season.
